newsitem.title: JAPAN: Samurai issues shrink after dollar's fall.
newsitem.headline: Samurai issues shrink after dollar's fall.

text.p: Samurai bond issues will hit their lowest level in two years this month as the dollar's recent fall against the yen has wiped out interest in dual-currency samurai bonds, underwriting sources said on Friday.

The popularity of the dual-currency issues boosted the overall volume of samurai issues to record levels recently, the sources said, but the fall in the dollar means none of the bonds will be issued in June, the first time that has happened since August 1995.
In the colourful language of the bond market, a samurai is not a traditional Japanese warrior but a bond issued in Japan by a non-Japanese borrower and denominated in yen.
On an issue-date basis, the overall samurai bond volume will fall to 82.5 billion yen ($723 million) in June, below the 100 billion yen ($877 million) level for the first time since May 1995.
"The samurai issuing volume will likely fall back to the levels it was at in mid-1995," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute.
"We won't see any issues of dual-currency samurai bonds for a while. Without them, the overall volume will not be as large as we've seen in recent years," he said.

Underwriters said overall samurai issues are expected to average about 100 billion yen ($877 million) or less a month, with borrowers from Asia, eastern European and other emerging markets likely to be the key fund-raisers.
In June, companies from Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea and Indonesia launched straight samurai bonds, with a South African sovereign issue also being launched.
The dual-currency samurai bonds were targeted at Japanese private investors, with most of the bonds selling out shortly after they went on sale, the underwriters said.

Those investors, seeking higher returns at a time of low interest rates at home, have felt comfortable about increasing their overseas investments because of the dollar's consistent appreciation against the yen over the past two years.
But the recent dive of the dollar has changed that, forcing brokerages to put off their plans to offer a huge volume of dual currency samurais, originally prepared for the summer bonus season.
During the June 1996 summer bonus season, samurai bond issues totalled 413 billion yen ($3.62 billion), of which dual-currency issues accounted for 220 billion yen ($1.92 billion).

Japanese retail investors' appetite for dual-currency bonds was huge throughout 1996, with volume amounting to 2.4 trillion yen ($21.0 billion) compared with the previous record of 600 billion yen ($5.26 billion) in 1995.

Underwriters said investors are now more cautious about purchasing foreign bonds heavily after experiencing losses from dual-currency samurai investments, unless the dollar stages a strong comeback against the yen.
Underwriters estimated that investors are holding more than 50 billion yen ($438 million) worth of currency losses from investments in dual-currency samurai bonds.
However, private investors are not expected to stop making foreign investments, or to shift their funds back into bank deposits or postal savings accounts again, underwriters said.

"Retail investors have learned a great deal about currency risks after experiencing huge losses from the dollar's plunge in May," an international finance manager at a major Japanese brokerage said. "But they are not expected to stop investing overseas. They'll continue diversifying their portfolios.
"This trend in the samurai market is only temporary until brokerages come up with new product that revives interest in the samurai market," he said. ($1=114 yen)
